item.title: Tiburon neighbors rally to find lost dog, bring him home
item.description: Apollo, a French bulldog-pug mix, broke his leash. A drone with thermal detection, a PawBoost listing and local volunteers all joined the two-day search.
item.content:encoded:
Apollo, a French bulldog-pug mix, was on a leash outside Mary Jasek’s Old Tiburon home Aug. 4, basking in the sun while she cleaned inside, when something spooked him. He bolted, Jasek says, “with such great force that he broke away from the leash.”

Jasek, who was dog-sitting for her daughter and son-in-law, ran through Old Tiburon’s hilly streets, searching and calling for him. She posted on Nextdoor, asking neighbors to watch for the dog.

The community responded almost immediately, she says.

“I had three people just show up in their car, look at me and roll their windows down and just say, … ‘Are you Mary?’” Jasek recalls. “And they said they were looking.”

Businesses put up lost-dog flyers, mail carriers watched for him and Tiburon Peninsula residents joined the search, in person and by sharing Jasek’s post online.

One of Jasek’s neighbors found Apollo two days later, Aug. 6, in Old St. Hilary’s Open Space Preserve and reunited him with Jasek, her daughter Dana Jasek and son-in-law Zachary D’Agostino of Marinwood.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Marinwood residents Dana Jasek and Zachary D’Agostino and Tiburon resident Mary Jasek, Dana’s mom, reunited with Apollo Aug. 6 following two days of searching after the dog broke from his leash and ran away while Mary Jasek was dog-sitting. (Francisco Martinez / The Ark)

item.title: Belvedere drops Mallard Pointe project manager
item.description: Belvedere has cut ties with the consulting firm it hired in April to oversee the Mallard Pointe redevelopment, weeks before demolition could begin on the 22-unit complex.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere has cut ties with the consulting firm it hired four months ago to oversee the Mallard Pointe redevelopment, leaving the city without a third-party project manager weeks before demolition could begin on the 22-unit lagoon-side complex.

The city contracted with Phillips Seabrook Associates of Santa Rosa on April 13 to oversee the 40-unit development on Belvedere Lagoon. The position was not optional: The conditions of approval the council attached to Mallard Pointe commit the city to retaining a part-time consultant to handle day-to-day coordination among the developer, city staff and residents, something residents had pressed the city for. Councilmembers discussed what they wanted from the role at their February retreat, and that feedback shaped the request for proposals. Three firms responded and all three were interviewed.

In an Aug. 10 newsletter, the city said it had decided to end its engagement with the firm.

Planning and Building Director Rebecca Markwick, answering questions by email, said the city reassessed its needs for the role and went looking for other firms with “a different mix of skills and expertise.” She said Aug. 14 that Belvedere was interviewing firms and expected to select a replacement within two weeks.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: New fitness studio approved for downtown Tiburon
item.description: Five Points Fitness plans free weights, cardio, self-adjusting strength machines and a recovery area with two kinds of saunas. The owners are targeting a February 2027 opening.
item.content:encoded:
A membership gym offering free weights, cardio equipment, self-adjusting strength machines and saunas is coming to a downtown Tiburon storefront that has sat empty since 2022.

The Tiburon Planning Commission on Aug. 12 granted Five Points Fitness a conditional-use permit to open an 8,090-square-foot gym across two floors at 1620 Tiburon Blvd. Recreation and entertainment uses are allowed in the property’s mixed-use zone only with a use permit, and the space had most recently been offices. The vote was 3-0, with Chair Daniel Amir and Vice Chair Eric Woodward absent. No one spoke during public comment.

Tom MacDonald, who co-owns the gym with Bryan LeFebure, said after the meeting that they’re targeting a February 2027 opening, pending construction permits and schedules.

The Tiburon location would be the company’s third. MacDonald told the commission that he and LeFebure bought the Corte Madera gym from World Gym about 21 years ago and have run the Novato gym for 11 years.

item.title: Tiburon Fire rejects grand jury timeline for consolidation talks
item.description: The Tiburon Fire Protection District board votedto partially disagree with all seven Marin County civil grand jury findings and to decline five of its nine recommendations.
item.content:encoded:
The Tiburon Fire Protection District board has told the Marin County civil grand jury it will not meet the jury’s deadlines for exploring consolidation with neighboring agencies, saying it will pursue shared services on its own schedule.

The board approved the district’s formal response 4-0 at its Aug. 12 meeting, with several minor additions and with board member Rick Jones absent. The response partially disagrees with all seven findings in the jury’s report, “Better Service at Lower Cost: Optimizing Essential Services for the Future of Marin,” and says the district will not implement five of the nine recommendations, which it called not warranted or not reasonable.

The report, released June 11, urged Marin’s more than 50 special districts — including fire, water, sanitation and refuse agencies — to accelerate consolidation talks, expand shared administrative services and publish standardized performance metrics. It said the county’s fragmented system duplicates administrative work, produces uneven costs and service levels and leaves some districts without the scale for long-term investment.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Report: Open creek sent skiers toward fatal avalanche path
item.description: Guides who led a Tiburon mother of three into a fatal Sierra avalanche were steering away from the slide path when an open creek turned them back, a commissioned report says.
item.content:encoded:
Guides who led a Tiburon mother of three into a fatal Sierra avalanche were steering the group away from the slide path when an open creek turned them back, according to a report their company commissioned.

The report does not say why the guides pressed on toward the trailhead after the crossing failed instead of returning to the huts they had left two hours earlier. Blackbird Mountain Guides, the Truckee company that ran the trip, has not addressed the question publicly.

Kate Morse, a 45-year-old biotech executive whose two eldest daughters compete for Sugar Bowl Academy, was one of six women killed in the Feb. 17 slide. They were part of a group of eight friends whose children ski for the academy near Donner Summit. Three guides died with them.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel

item.title: Mildred Frances Minter (Milly) Jewell
item.description: Former Tiburon resident Mildred Frances Minter (Milly) Jewell, age 102, died July 3, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Former Tiburon resident Mildred Frances Minter (Milly) Jewell, age 102, died peacefully with her daughters at her side on July 3, 2026, at her home in The Tamalpais/Sequoia Living senior residence in Greenbrae, California.

Milly Jewell was born on April 25, 1924, in Cedar County, Missouri, to Virgil Artemis Minter and Ada Byrd Minter (née Reid). She earned her bachelor’s degree in journalism from the University of Missouri at Columbia, then moved to Chicago to work in communications for the National Safety Council. In Chicago, she met her future husband, Albert Hartwell Jewell Jr., then a medical student at Northwestern. They married in 1952 during Dr. Jewell’s surgery residency in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and moved to Marin County, California, in 1959.

Milly was a homemaker and active local volunteer. In the early 1970s, she spearheaded a drive to get a produce truck to come to her neighborhood so neighbors could buy produce directly from the farmers — a precursor to CSA farm boxes. With her keen interest in good food and trying new recipes, she cooked her way through Julia Child’s “Mastering the Art of French Cooking.” She volunteered in the Reed schools, her daughters’ Girl Scout troops, the Marin Art & Garden Center, the Marin County Free Library, the Tiburon Landmarks Society, and the Culinary Carnival, an annual event to raise money for Children’s Garden. She was also a longtime supporter of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco and the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts.

With her husband, Milly made numerous opera-focused trips to Europe and travelled as well in Asia and Australia. In her later years, she hiked in the Sierras and abroad, and frequently walked the Tiburon bike path with her Belvedere and Tiburon friends, who informally called their group “The Fallen Arches.” After she and her husband moved to The Tamalpais in 1997, she became an avid player of bridge, Chinese-style Mahjongg, and gin rummy. Throughout her life, Milly was a voracious reader, often reading three books a week. The last book she finished, in the weeks before her death, was the just-published novel “Whistler” by Ann Patchett. She especially enjoyed poetry, writing some of her own and memorizing the poetry of others. She often had the perfect impromptu quote from Shakespeare, Alexander Pope, or Rilke (and, at parties, Ogden Nash or a limerick or two). Above all, she was devoted to each of her three grandsons, with whom she enjoyed close individual re...

item.title: Janet Anne Benson (“Jan”) Pickett
item.description: Janet Anne Benson (“Jan”) Pickett, a Tiburon resident for over 40 years, passed away peacefully at her home on June 23, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Janet Anne Benson (“Jan”) Pickett, a Tiburon resident for over 40 years, passed away peacefully at her home on June 23, 2026, surrounded by her family after a courageous and lengthy battle with lung disease. Jan lived a beautiful, loving, and extraordinary life, and will be deeply missed by everyone who knew her.

Jan was born in Chicago on March 20, 1951, to John William and Mary Halpin Benson. She graduated from the University of Illinois with a B.A. degree, and she obtained master’s degrees from Southern Connecticut University in education and from the University of San Francisco in psychology. Jan was a teacher, a marriage and child counselor, and served as president of the Reed Union School District. Jan met her future husband Donn in grammar school (assuredly neither of them had the foggiest notion of any future together). They married right after their college graduations in 1973, and that special union endured for 53 years.

Jan’s true passion was being a mother and grandmother. She was a beloved and enduring matriarch — selfless, patient, caring, kind, wise, and unwaveringly positive. She will be remembered lovingly by her family and friends for so many of her unique contributions to their lives — her unceasing dedication and support of her ‘ohana. She had a special relationship to Hawaii and its aloha spirit.

Jan was renowned for her gift of throwing unforgettable and unique parties, her baking, particularly Christmas cookies (and as a teenager she won the first prize in a Northern Illinois cherry pie contest!); her hiking the hills above her home in Tiburon, especially to enjoy the poppies and other wildflowers; her Swedish Christmas celebrations to honor her heritage; her passion for playing charades and dice games; her loyalty to the Giants through thick and thin; her love of British police dramas; her special ability to grow beautiful gardens, particularly roses and dahlias; her sunrise walks along Lanikai Beach; her special Cosmo recipe; and her love of fireworks and Tahoe — best in combination. Jan also loved to travel and explore the world. She and Donn visited more than 65 countries while traveling to every continent, and (a particular Jan favorite) they took part in over 100 safari game drives during six trips to Africa.

Jan is survived by her husband, Donn; her daughter, Jessica (Parker) Lyons; her son, William (Emma) Pickett; four grandchildren, Johanna and Lillian Pickett, and Rose and Harvey Lyons; and he...

item.title: Garden Plot: Dragonflies bring beauty and benefits to local gardens
item.description: Dragonflies are carnivores that eat aphids, gnats, mosquitoes and flies, which makes them worth having around.
item.content:encoded:
Are you lucky enough to have dragonflies in your garden, or maybe have you seen them near fresh water such as the marsh behind the Belvedere-Tiburon Library? They are stunningly beautiful. I have a seasonal stream that seems to trickle all summer these days, so they’re around my garden, sometimes flying close to observe what I’m up to out there. There are some large dragonflies that are bright red, smaller ones that are a brilliant blue and some that are grayish. All are so much fun to watch.

Like bees and other insects, dragonflies have what appear to be huge eyes, which are actually compound eyes consisting of thousands of simple eyes. Fortunately, they’re harmless to us and don’t sting. Damselflies are the smaller ones; they have wings that fold into the shape of a V or over their backs when they are resting. Larger ones, called darners, have wings at right angles to their sides, and some can approach the size of a hummingbird.
item.dc:creator: Diane Lynch
item.media:description: This dragonfly, called a darner, is characterized by wings that are perpendicular to the body. The stream in my garden, shown here in winter, has a catch basin at the bottom where the dragonflies hang out in summer. (Diane Lynch / For The Ark)

item.title: Picks of the Week: Bluegrass at Old St. Hilary's; Tiburon, Strawberry festivals
item.description: Strawberry Rec's Community Night and the Tiburon chamber's Friday Nights on Main are Aug. 21, while Charlie Torch will play a bluegrass concert Aug. 23.
item.content:encoded:
Bluegrass band Charlie Torch at Old St. Hilary’s:Charlie Torch will play a bluegrass concert at 4 p.m. Aug. 23 at Old St. Hilary’s Landmark in Tiburon. The group is a family affair, with fiddle player Chad Manning and his daughters Jayne Manning on guitar and Jasper Manning on mandolin, plus Tyler Stegall on banjo and Mark Schatz on bass. Tickets are $20-$25 in advance online or at the Landmarks Society office, $25-$30 at the door if not sold out. There is no parking at Old St. Hilary’s Landmark; free parking is at The Boardwalk shopping center, with a shuttle leaving from in front of Rustic Bakery beginning half an hour before the show. 415-435-1853 orlandmarkssociety.com.

Two community festivals Friday night:There are two local events Aug. 21 for getting out and mingling with your neighbors. The final Friday Nights on Main of the summer runs 5:30-8:30 p.m., with Main Street in Tiburon closed to car traffic for outdoor dining from local restaurants, live music, games, a photo booth and face painting. 415-435-5633 ortiburonchamber.org. At the Strawberry Recreation Center, Community Night, 4:30-8 p.m., will have a selection of vendors, booths from community groups, food trucks and family activities including a climbing wall and bounce house. Bring low seating for a picnic on the field. No dogs are allowed. 415-383-6494 orstrawberry.marin.org. Both events are free.

item.title: Tartine Bakery Tartine opens its doors at Strawberry Village
item.description: San Francisco's Tartine Bakery formally opens its first North Bay store today, Aug. 19, at Strawberry Village shopping center.
item.content:encoded:
Updated:12 minutes ago

Tiburon Peninsula residents no longer have to drive to San Francisco, or wait in its hourlong lines, for aTartinecountry loaf.

The bakery formally opens its first North Bay store today, Aug. 19, at the Strawberry Village shopping center, filling two storefronts that had sat empty for years.

The wait began when Tartine announced the location in March 2025.

The 3,091-square-foot bakery and cafe sits in the same cluster as Safeway, Calico Corners and High Tech Burrito. It is open 8 a.m.-4 p.m. daily.

The menu carries the sourdough, morning buns and pastries that built the brand, along with soft-scramble tartines, breakfast sandwiches on a sweet potato bun and coffee. Lunch items include salads, ham-and-Gruyere sandwiches and a double smash burger with American cheese, celery remoulade and fennel confit.

The bread is baked in San Francisco and delivered daily. Pastries are made fresh in Strawberry.

Tartine has been serving customers intermittently since Aug. 13, opening and closing as staff trained ahead of today’s official opening.

A line formed outside before the doors opened at 8 a.m. Aug. 17, and the cafe was full by 8:30. Mark Jensen of Kentfield and Santiago Sciutti of San Rafael rode up on bikes, trying Tartine for the first time. Julia and Anthony Lugo of Mill Valley, Tartine customers in San Francisco for years, said they had followed the opening on Instagram.

Cashier Grace Tigrero said lines formed outside on Aug. 15 and Aug. 16 as well, and that the bakery sold out of baked goods within a few hours both days.

“Opening our first location in Marin has long been a goal,” Tartine CEO Dar Vasseghi said in an Aug. 14 statement. “Strawberry Village is an ideal home for us — a neighborhood gathering place with a strong sense of community. People have been asking us for this for a long time, and we’re excited to deliver on that demand.”

San Francisco firm Studio BBA designed the space to pick up the shopping center’s Mediterranean look, with high ceilings, an open floor plan and sightlines that let customers watch the bakers work. It seats 120 people indoors and out.

The store is also a return to the peninsula’s doorstep for a business that started nearby. Founders Chad Robertson and Elisabeth Prueitt began baking at Bay Village Bread in Point Reyes Station in 1999, then moved to 17 Madrona St. in Mill Valley in 2000. They left for San Francisco in 2...
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel
item.media:description: Cashier Grace Tigrero waits on Mark Jensen and Santiago Sciutti on Aug. 17 at Tartine Bakery in Strawberry Village. Jensen, of Kentfield, and Sciutti, of San Rafael, rode their bikes over to try Tartine for the first time. (Ted McDonnell / For The Ark)

Bagged country, rye and oat-porridge loaves wait for customers on Aug. 17 at Tartine Bakery in Strawberry Village, where all the breads are sourdough. The bakery has been serving customers since Aug. 13 and holds its official opening today, Aug. 19. (Ted McDonnell / For The Ark)
James Weinbaum of Tiburon eats a sticky bun on Aug. 17 at Tartine Bakery in Strawberry Village during its soft opening. (Ted McDonnell / For The Ark)

item.title: Tiburon to spend $250k to dig out of audit backlog
item.description: Tiburon will spend up to $250,000 on outside accountants to clear a three-year backlog of unfinished financial audits.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon will spend up to $250,000 on outside accountants to clear a three-year backlog of unfinished financial audits, work that isn’t expected to leave the town current until the middle of 2027 at the earliest.

The Town Council voted 4-0 on Aug. 5 to approve a $195,000 contract with Rogers Anderson Malody & Scott, a San Bernardino accounting firm known as RAMS, to help finish audits for fiscal years 2023-2024, 2024-2025 and 2025-2026. Councilmember Holli Thier, who attended by videoconference, was no longer on the call when the vote was taken.

It is the second agreement the town has signed with the firm. Town Manager Greg Chanis approved an initial $55,000 contract in July under his own signing authority, below the amount that requires council approval. Neither needed a budget amendment, because the current fiscal year 2026-2027 budget already carried money for the work. That money had been going to Regional Government Services, which had provided the town’s finance and accounting help until Tiburon dropped it in July. Chanis said after the meeting that ending that contract cost the town nothing.

The oldest audit, covering fiscal 2024, is scheduled to begin Aug. 17, with financial statements presented to the council by the end of October, Chanis said. The fiscal 2025 audit is projected for January to March 2027, and fiscal 2026, the year that ended June 30, for April to June 2027. The town would be caught up by late July 2027 at the latest.

Much of the delay is a scheduling problem. September through December is the busy season for municipal audits and firms are typically booked solid, Chanis said, adding that the town would keep looking for chances to shorten the turnaround. The town’s auditor, The Pun Group of Santa Ana, works alongside RAMS for several other government agencies, a relationship Chanis credited with securing the Aug. 17 start date quickly. He said The Pun Group has also put Tiburon at the top of its list for any opening.

“If their schedule changes or if one of their current customers drops out, and there’s — a slot opens up, we’d be able to move faster on the subsequent audits,” Chanis said.

The $195,000 buys more than audit help. Under the firm’s proposal, it also covers writing standard operating procedures, reviewing internal-control problems The Pun Group flagged in fiscal years 2021-2022 through 2023-2024, auditing who has access to the town’s financial software and cross-training staff.<...
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez

item.title: Belvedere finds shoreline building it never approved
item.description: Belvedere planning officials walking the shoreline at low tide in March found a two-story building on Beach Road the city says it never approved.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere planning officials walking the shoreline at low tide in March found a two-story building standing at the water’s edge on Beach Road that the city says it never approved. More than four months later, the owner still hasn’t responded.

Building Inspector Genaro Muniz posted a stop-work order on the exterior of the main house at 344 Beach Road on March 25. It says work on the structure was found “not to comply or to be deficient” for a single reason: “For building an illegal structure without Planning or Building Dept. approval.”

The city then obtained photographs from a resident that appear to document the sequence. Images taken in August and September 2024 show the shoreline below the main house with no second building on it. Photos from February 2025 show a two-story structure under construction, sheathed in housewrap with its windows set and scaffolding along one side. Photos taken March 23 show the same building finished — flat-roofed, painted and glassed in on two floors, its lower wall rising from the stone seawall a few feet above the tideline.

Planning and Building Director Rebecca Markwick Markwick said basic details — height, square footage and how the building is being used — remain unknown because the site can’t be seen from Beach Road and the owner has not discussed the work with the city.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: In 2024 (left), the seawall below the main house at 344 Beach Road held no second structure beside the property’s dock. By this March (right), a flat-roofed two-story building stood in that spot, painted and glassed in on both floors. Belvedere posted a stop-work order on the main house March 25 over what it called an illegal structure built without planning or building approval. The owner has not responded to the city. (via city of Belvedere)

item.title: ‘Birdhouse,’ basket swings in mix for Cypress Hollow Park
item.description: Basket swings, a birdhouse climbing structure and wooden towers with slides are among options Tiburon is weighing for a rebuilt Cypress Hollow playground.
item.content:encoded:
Tire and basket swings, a climbing structure shaped like a birdhouse and wooden play towers with slides are among the options Tiburon is weighing for a rebuilt playground at Cypress Hollow Park.

Members of the Tiburon Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission’s mini-parks subcommittee presented preliminary concepts from three playground-equipment vendors at an in-person workshop July 28 and a virtual workshop Aug. 4.

The designs and the feedback on them will be folded into the 60%-completed design set that Santa Rosa-based park designer Carlile Macy is preparing for the commission’s special meeting at 6 p.m. Aug. 24, subcommittee member and parks Commissioner Chuck Hornbrook said during the Aug. 4 session.

Hornbrook said structures can be mixed and matched across manufacturers for the park’s new play area of roughly 3,000 square feet, a 50% increase over the 2,000 square feet of play space at the half-acre park now.

Even with the expansion, Hornbrook said, the park’s size limits which marquee structures will fit. He said the Bel Aire play area covers 0.7 acres and South of the Knoll Park about 6.5 acres.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: A rendering from Earthscape Play shows a basket swing among preliminary options for a rebuilt playground at Cypress Hollow Park. The Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission’s mini-parks subcommittee presented concepts from three vendors at workshops July 28 and Aug. 4. No design has been chosen, and no construction has been approved.

item.title: Tiburon real-estate broker turned rocker releases his third album
item.description: Dan Mihalovich spent his teens at The Fillmore. Now the Tiburon commercial real-estate broker has released his third album under the name Dan Moss.
item.content:encoded:
Dan Mihalovich spent his formative teen years at The Fillmore in San Francisco, drawing inspiration from the rock legends who took the stage and immersing himself in the venue’s counterculture vibe.

“I think I’m always looking for that kind of electrifying connection, if you can find it, with bands or music,” Mihal­ovich says.

Inspired by acts like Janis Joplin, Jimi Hendrix and The Beatles, Mihalovich picked up a guitar at age 12 and dreamed of a life in rock ’n’ roll.

While he established his career in commercial real estate, music remained a lifelong hobby — until about six years ago, when Mihalovich decided he wanted to turn his passion into a second career. Music, he says, uses a different part of his brain.

“I think a lot of what we do in our daily lives suppresses that kind of brain activity,” he says. “After working in the commercial real estate for so long, I got to a point where I just didn’t love doing it anymore. And I thought that, all of that brain activity is really interfering with what I really want to do.”

He’s since released three albums under his stage name, Dan Moss. The most recent, “Blueberry Blonde,” was released in July on Spotify and Apple Music and on vinyl.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: Tiburon resident Dan Mihalovich holds his custom Gibson Les Paul Aug. 4 at The Boardwalk shopping center, wearing a shirt bearing the cover art from his third album, ‘Blueberry Blonde.’ He released the album in July under the name Dan Moss and will play a release party Oct. 23 at Peri’s Tavern in Fairfax. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Tiburon council sends home expansion back for design review
item.description: Three neighbors appealed the approval, saying the 794-square-foot addition would block their views and that the board never seriously weighed building down.
item.content:encoded:
The Tiburon Town Council has sent a Hawthorne Terrace couple’s home expansion back to the Design Review Board, ordering a closer look at whether the project can be built lower to spare neighbors’ views.

The council voted 3-1 on Aug. 5 to return the proposed 794-square-foot expansion at 700 Hawthorne Drive to the board, instructing it to scrutinize alternatives to the height increase and to gather better visual evidence of how neighbors would be affected.

The move came after the council heard separate appeals from three neighbors: Kamran Shirazi of 3 Rock Hill Road, Ryan Lee of 699 Hawthorne Drive and Neda Shafaghi of 705 Hawthorne Drive. They sought to overturn the design board’s approval of the plans submitted by homeowners Eric Tiret and Caely Cusick.

Councilmember Holli Thier cast the opposing vote, saying she felt neighbor sentiment was substantial enough to fully grant the neighbors’ appeals and overturn the project approval. Councilmember Jack Ryan recused himself because he owns property within 500 feet of Cusick and Tiret’s home.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: The view from 699 Hawthorne Drive looks across the roofline of 700 Hawthorne Drive toward Richardson Bay and Sausalito. Ryan Lee, one of three neighbors who appealed, said the proposed addition would cut into the sight line from his great room. The Town Council on Aug. 5 sent the project back to the Design Review Board, which had approved it in April on conditions that included removing the red-leafed photinia shrub at center right. (Ryan Lee via town of Tiburon)

item.title: New Business: Marin Service Course opens new bike shop at The Boardwalk
item.description: Marin Service Course, owned by Tiburon's Peter Lucas, has opened a second location at The Boardwalk.
item.content:encoded:
While growing up on Centro West Street, Peter Lucas would turn his daily bike ride to Del Mar Middle School into an adventure.

He says he used to “bomb down the hill” that descends from Old St. Hilary’s Landmark. Then it was time for tricks.

“I would try and wheelie the whole way to Del Mar school,” he says.

Lucas’ love for biking hasn’t waned, and now the Tiburon resident is aiming to share his passion with the community. Lucas openedMarin Service Courseat The Boardwalk shopping center July 25. It’s the business’s second location, following the original Fairfax shop that opened in 2019. The Tiburon outpost replaces Diana’s of Tiburon, the gift shop that closed in April 2025 after owner Diana Maureen decided to retire.

Marin Service Course sells and services bikes and stocks nutrition products for cyclists, and it offers bike fitting, coaching and organized community rides.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: Peter Lucas opened Marin Service Course at The Boardwalk shopping center July 25, the second location for the bike shop he founded in Fairfax in 2019. Lucas, who grew up on Centro West Street riding to Del Mar Middle School, built the store around a bar, at rear, where customers can drink free espresso and watch races. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Everyday Encounters: A passion for Italy inspires chocolatier’s small-batch bonbons
item.description: John Cruger makes small-batch Italian-inspired bonbons in Tiburon and sells them at one place: the Paradise Coffee cart at Point Tiburon Plaza.
item.content:encoded:
John Cruger is the man behind a selection of sweet treats that can be found only on Tiburon Boulevard.

At Paradise Coffee, the mobile coffee cart at Point Tiburon Plaza, customers can buy items from Cruger’s small-batch chocolate line, which he calls Gio Dolce. There are bonbons with flavors like Aperol, espresso martini and cinnamon, as well as what Cruger calls his masterpiece: a “cafe mocha” chocolate shaped like a tiny Starbucks cup with three layers — dark chocolate, caramel chocolate and white chocolate cheesecake — all held together with a swirl of espresso syrup.

“The bonbons are real shiny, kind of like pearls,” he says while walking his dog along Shoreline Park Aug. 7. “And they’re all Italian inspired and they’re all inspired by the Amalfi Coast.”

Cruger, 61, makes the bonbons himself in Tiburon, buying chocolate from Switzerland and cocoa butter from the United Kingdom, then using ingredients sourced from Northern California for the fillings and flavorings. The result is a small-batch operation shaped by the climate as much as the recipe.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Jean Barnett
item.description: Jean Barnett, age 94, passed away in Santa Rosa on July 12, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Jean Barnett, age 94, passed away in Santa Rosa on July 12, 2026, after a brief illness following a long battle with dementia.

Jean was preceded in death by her beloved husband, James Barnett, with whom she shared 63 years of marriage before his passing in 2020. Together they built a life centered on family, friendship, and a love of the outdoors.

Born and raised in Sebastopol and educated at Stanford, Jean spent her adult years in Marin County, where she devoted herself to raising her family and embracing the natural beauty of California. She found joy in nature, travel, golf, gardening, and watercolor painting, pursuits that reflected her curiosity, creativity, and appreciation for the world around her.

Jean was known for her warmth and generosity of spirit. She always had a friendly smile and a kind word to share, and her genuine interest in others made her a lifelong friend to many. Her quiet kindness and gracious presence touched countless lives and will be remembered by all who knew her.

She is survived by her sister Doreen, sons Charlie and Michael, and her grandchildren, Kyle and Nora, who will cherish her memory and carry forward the values of kindness, friendship, and appreciation for life’s simple pleasures that she embodied so well.

Jean’s family takes comfort in the many wonderful memories she leaves behind and in the lasting impact she had on the lives of those fortunate enough to know and love her.

item.title: A Life Well Lived: Norman Allen Spencer
item.description: Norman Allen Spencer passed away peacefully at his home in Tiburon, California, on July 20, 2026, at the age of 83.
item.content:encoded:
Norman Allen Spencer passed away peacefully at his home in Tiburon, California, on July 20, 2026, at the age of 83. While his family grieves his loss, they celebrate a life that was rich in love, friendship, and purpose.

Born on August 5, 1942, in Seattle, Washington, to Henry Norman Spencer and Mary Elva Dillingham Spencer, Norm grew up in the Pacific Northwest. He graduated from Roosevelt High School before earning his degree from the University of Washington in 1964.

In 1968, Norm met Sally Kolthoff in San Francisco, where they married in 1974 before moving to Tiburon in 1975. Together they shared 52 wonderful years of marriage, raising a family, traveling, and enjoying life together.

Norm enjoyed an extraordinary 41-year career in commercial real estate — a profession he loved and often said he never considered “work.” He began at Coldwell Banker, where he introduced Hines to the opportunity that became the iconic 101 California St. It marked the beginning of his distinguished career with Hines, where he spent more than 25 years as an executive in the San Francisco office.

At Hines, Norm was known not only for his expertise and professionalism, but also for his integrity, warmth, and ability to build lasting relationships. He retired in 2010 after contributing to many renowned office buildings throughout Northern and Southern California. To Norm, however, the greatest reward of his career was never the buildings themselves — it was the friendships he made along the way.

At the height of his commercial real-estate career, Norm pursued his interest in viticulture at UC Davis, inspired by his growing passion for wine. This led to the creation of Spencer Vineyards in Oakville, where they built a family home that became the backdrop for more than three decades of family dinners, milestone celebrations, summer weekends, and treasured traditions.

Outside the office, Norm embraced life with enthusiasm. Golf was one of his greatest joys, but not because of the score. As a proud member of Meadow Club, Kohanaiki, Summit Muni, and formerly the Olympic Club and Silverado, he treasured the camaraderie, the opportunity to win a few dollars, and the friendships forged over 18 holes. His favorite course was never defined by its scenery — it was wherever he happened to be playing with his buddies, his son Greg, or his grandson Spencer.

item.title: Marin artists pay tribute to the spirit of America in ‘We the People’
item.description: Eight local artists are showing work at Tiburon Town Hall in "We the People," an exhibit marking the 250th anniversary of U.S. independence.
item.content:encoded:
Eight local artists are featured in “We the People,” a Tiburon Town Hall exhibition designed to celebrate the 250th anniversary of U.S. independence.

The exhibit, sponsored by the Heritage & Arts Commission, runs through Aug. 31 in Town Hall’s downstairs gallery. The commission put out an open call earlier this summer inviting peninsula residents of all ages to submit works across all mediums that “explore historical events, cultural traditions, landscapes, everyday life, national symbols or personal narratives that speak to the spirit of America.”
item.dc:creator: Diane Smith
item.media:description: ‘Stand Up for Democracy!’ is a mixed-media piece by Jeri Brittell of Tiburon, on display through Aug. 31 in the downstairs gallery at Tiburon Town Hall as part of ‘We the People.’ The exhibition features work by eight local artists marking the 250th anniversary of U.S. independence. (via Jeri Brittell)
